extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, and comedians interested in the history, practices, and cultural impact of The Comedy Store and stand-up industry
extracted.subtask_description: Documenting the history, operations, labor practices, and cultural significance of a single comedy club (The Comedy Store). Focuses on venue features, notable alumni, labor disputes, and the club's role as a training/showcase venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay/compensation policy (no-pay policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Until 1979 neither Shore nor Friedman paid comedians a salary; the theory was that comedians should almost be paying the owners for the exposure the clubs provided (described on the page as a 'no-pay policy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context and consequences: the no-pay policy led to dissatisfaction and a 1979 job action/unionization attempt. The page describes the owners' view that the club was a showcase/training ground rather than a profit-driven payroll, and notes that after the dispute comedians in Los Angeles began to be paid for their shows. Example/anti-pattern: operating a club under the assumption that exposure substitutes for pay can provoke protests and union activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue function as a showcase/training ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitzi Shore argued that the club was and had always been a showcase and training ground for young comedians and was not about profits; comedians could work on material in front of casting agents and talent scouts who might hire them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as an evaluative criterion: a club's value may be judged by how well it provides a platform for developing material and visibility to industry scouts. The page frames this as a justification for unpaid or low-paid appearances and as part of the club's cultural role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer legal classification (independent contractor vs employee)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comedians were classified as 'independent contractors' and were not under contract with the club; legally this meant the 1979 job action was not a strike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational and legal implications: classification affects labor rights, the ability to strike, and obligations of the venue. The page uses this point to explain why the job action wasn't legally a strike and how disputes were shaped by classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment model after labor action (flat rate per performance / paid regulars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the dispute, the deal allowed comics to be classified as independent contractors while paying them a flat rate per performance; later references note 'Paid Regulars' at The Comedy Store.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical model guidance: venues can adopt a flat fee per set and designate paid regulars. The page documents this as the historical resolution and links it to later operational practices (e.g., program of paid regulars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue capacity, facilities, and renovations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comedy Store opened with a 99-seat theatre, was renovated/expanded (Mitzi Shore renovated and expanded the club to include a 450-seat main room), and later included additional locations/rooms (Playhouse, Westwood, La Jolla, Sheraton Universal, Las Vegas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative metric, capacity and facilities (number/size of rooms, renovations, associated venues) indicate a club's scale and ability to host larger acts, specials, or events. The page uses these facts to chart growth and prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of residential/support spaces for talent development (Cresthill house)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitzi Shore owned a 5,000-square-foot house (Cresthill) near the club where comedians lived/partied in the late 1970s–1980s; it served as an incubator for developing acts and was later converted into a recovery house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates another dimension by which a venue can nurture talent: providing residence or communal spaces contributes to career development (but can also produce negative social consequences). The page provides examples of comedians who lived there and how it influenced their acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notable alumni / roster as measure of significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The article lists numerous notable performers (e.g., Jay Leno, David Letterman, Richard Pryor, Robin Williams, Chris Rock, Jerry Seinfeld, etc.), implying the club's importance by the prominence of alumni.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A club's reputation and historical impact can be evaluated by the success and fame of comedians who performed there. The page explicitly uses a long list of alumni to demonstrate cultural influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hosting media specials and documentaries (HBO specials, Showtime docu-series)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comedy Store served as host location for annual HBO Young Comedians specials beginning in 1979 and is the subject of a Showtime docu-series (debuted October 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hosting televised specials and being the subject of documentary media are indicators of a venue's prominence and cultural reach. The page cites these media appearances as milestones in the club's history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor relations and public protests as part of venue evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1979 strike/unionization attempts (Comedians for Compensation), six-week protest/picketing, crossing of picket lines by some famous comedians, and later dissolution of the union in 1980 are described in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labor history is relevant to assessing a venue's practices, ethics, and relationship with performers. The article uses these events to contextualize changes in payment and industry norms; they serve as cautionary examples of the consequences of certain managerial policies.
